element_analysis.subject: text block at top
element_analysis.evidence: Lines of brown and red script run across the top edge of the page, partly cropped. Transcribed as far as legible: "ist tem weil der ein stunde als in diser spere gestehen stet". The sun-like face with red rays is directly below it.

element_analysis.subject: Cor?
element_analysis.evidence: Free-standing red text just to the left of the red-rayed face, slightly higher than the face's centre. It is not joined to the face by any line. No allowed predicate describes 'left of', so 'above' is the closest.

element_analysis.subject: sohs
element_analysis.evidence: Free-standing red text just to the right of the red-rayed face, slightly higher than the face's centre. It is not joined by any line. 'Above' is the closest allowed predicate for this side-by-side position.

element_analysis.subject: sun-like face with red rays
element_analysis.evidence: A round face with eyes, nose and mouth is drawn inside a circle edged with pointed red rays. The lower rays touch the top of the hatched outer band. A thin vertical line passes through the face and continues to the centre of the diagram.

element_analysis.subject: left crescent
element_analysis.evidence: A brown-filled crescent with a red outline, opening to the right, lies at the left edge. Its inner curve touches the left side of the hatched outer band. A thin horizontal line runs from the star through the crescent towards the centre.

element_analysis.subject: small star outline (left)
element_analysis.evidence: A faint, small star-shaped outline in thin brown line lies to the left of the left crescent. The same thin horizontal line appears to pass through it and on to the crescent.

element_analysis.subject: right crescent
element_analysis.evidence: A brown-filled crescent with a red outline, opening to the left, lies at the right edge. Its inner curve touches the right side of the hatched outer band. A thin horizontal line runs from the centre to it.

element_analysis.subject: inner circle
element_analysis.evidence: A thin brown circle lies concentric within the outer ring, which is filled with short radial tick marks (hatching). Two concentric circles bound the hatched band.

element_analysis.subject: numerals around the ring
element_analysis.evidence: Numerals sit in the space between the inner circle and the hatched band, each with a small red or brown dot beside it. They run around the full circumference, one per sector. Legible readings include "8", "9", "10", "11", "18", "19", "20", "21", "22", "23", "1". The others are partly [illegible].

element_analysis.subject: [illegible]dies
element_analysis.evidence: Red text written vertically, with the letters stacked, in the upper part of the inner circle above the centre. Only the ending "dies" is reasonably legible. The rest is [illegible].

element_analysis.subject: Oriens
element_analysis.evidence: Red text, read horizontally, in the left part of the inner circle, to the left of the central circle.

element_analysis.subject: Orrid[illegible]
element_analysis.evidence: Red text, read horizontally, in the right part of the inner circle, to the right of the central circle. The end of the word is crossed by a thin line and is [illegible].

element_analysis.subject: Sep[illegible]
element_analysis.evidence: Red text written vertically, with the letters stacked, in the lower part of the inner circle below the centre. Only the beginning "Sep" is reasonably legible. The rest is [illegible].

element_analysis.subject: central circle
element_analysis.evidence: A small brown-filled circle with a red outline sits at the exact centre of the diagram. It has a small dark point in the middle.

element_analysis.subject: radial lines
element_analysis.evidence: Many thin brown straight lines run outwards from the central circle, dividing the rings into equal sectors. They cross the inner circle and reach the hatched band. Some continue slightly beyond it.

element_analysis.subject: short red radial strokes outside the band
element_analysis.evidence: Short red strokes are spaced around the outside of the hatched band, pointing radially. Some seem to continue as thin lines towards the band, but most do not touch it.

element_analysis.subject: bottom circle with brown fill
element_analysis.evidence: At the bottom is a circle with a red outline and a brown ring, with a paler centre containing a faint cross-like mark and traces of a face. It lies just below the hatched band without clearly touching it.

element_analysis.subject: Nox
element_analysis.evidence: Free-standing red text centred below the bottom circle, with a red dot before it.

element_analysis.subject: red stamp (lower left)
element_analysis.evidence: In the lower left corner of the page is a faint red stamp showing a crown shape with a few letters. It lies outside the diagram, below and to the left of the hatched band.

interpretation.diagram_classification: cosmological / astronomical-computistical diagram (a 24-hour day and night diagram, probably a horary or time-reckoning scheme)
interpretation.interpretation: The diagram most likely shows the division of the natural day into 24 hours, in the form of a wheel. A central earth-like disc stands inside a circle divided into 24 sectors by radial lines. Numerals are written around the ring. The sun at the top and the dark circle with "Nox" at the bottom mark the opposite points of day and night. The two crescents at the sides probably stand for the moon, or for the changing light at the horizon. The four words inside the inner circle, "Oriens", "Orrid[illegible]" (probably Occidens), and the vertically written words at top and bottom (probably Meridies and Septentrio), mark the four cardinal directions. The whole scheme joins the cycle of hours, the movement of the sun and the orientation of the heavens in one image. The German text at the top ("ist tem weil der ein stunde als in diser spere gestehen stet", approximately 'this is the time of one hour as it stands in this sphere') suggests it is part of a vernacular astronomical or astrological treatise and explains how an hour is represented in the sphere.
interpretation.evidence: Written in the diagram: the labels "Oriens" (left), "Nox" (bottom), "sohs" (probably sol, next to the sun), "Cor?" (reading uncertain), the vertical words ending in "dies" and beginning with "Sep", and the German line above that mentions "stunde" (hour) and "spere" (sphere). Visible: 24 radial sectors, with numerals running from 1 to 23 around the ring, a hatched outer band, a sun-like face with rays at the top, a dark circle at the bottom and a crescent on each side. External knowledge: medieval computistical and astronomical manuscripts often use wheel diagrams for the hours and the four cardinal directions. Some readings are unsure. Step 1 gives "[illegible]dies" and "Sep[illegible]" while the completions to Meridies and Septentrio are inferred. Orrid[illegible] is an uncertain reading and may be Occidens. "Cor?" and "sohs" are uncertain readings and the Step 1 predicates for them ("above") are only approximate, since the texts stand beside the sun. The Step 1 entry for the red stamp, which is a library mark and not part of the diagram, is also not an element of the diagram's meaning.

interpretation.diagram_classification: cosmological (sun, moon and the cardinal directions in an hour wheel)
interpretation.interpretation: The elements outside the wheel are the heavenly bodies in the order of the day. The sun, drawn as a face with red rays, stands at the top at the position of midday. The dark circle with a faint face-like mark at the bottom, labelled "Nox", stands at the position of midnight. The crescents at left and right probably show the moon, or the two horizons at which the luminaries rise and set, at the east ("Oriens") and west positions. The short red strokes around the band seem to be rays of light spreading from the sun, or marks of the hours. The small star outline to the left of the left crescent may be a star or planet sign, and is uncertain. The central circle, with its centre point from which the radial lines start, is the earth or the centre of the sphere, from which the sectors of the hours are measured.
interpretation.evidence: Visible: the rayed face at the top, the dark circle at the bottom with the red text "Nox" below it, the two crescents with red outlines and brown fill at the left and right edges, the star outline on the left, the short red strokes around the band, and the small central circle from which all the radial lines start. External: sun and night/moon at opposite poles of a wheel is a common way of showing a day cycle. The identification of the crescents with the moon and of the central circle with the earth is an inference. The Step 1 relations for these figures ("connected_to" the hatched band, and the star connected to the crescent) are uncertain, because the figures often only touch or stand next to the band. The Step 1 reading of the bottom circle as a face is also uncertain.
